mercy_translation.text:
One might especially be astonished at the Greeks, who laugh at things that are not laughable while remaining blind to their own shame, which they set up in stones and wood and fail to see.

Yet since our argument is not lacking in demonstrations, let us also put them to shame by reasonable considerations, especially from things we ourselves also observe. What is absurd in what we say, or what deserves mockery? Is it simply that we say the Word has appeared in a body? If they become friends of truth, they themselves will agree that this did not happen absurdly.

If they altogether deny that there is a Word of God, they act superfluously in mocking what they do not know.

But if they confess that there is a Word of God, that he is ruler of the universe, that in him the Father created the world, that through his providence all things are enlightened, given life, and sustained, and that he reigns over all so that from the works of providence he is known and through him the Father—then consider, I ask, whether they do not unknowingly turn their mockery against themselves.

The philosophers of the Greeks say that the world is a great body, and in this they speak truly. For we see it and its parts falling under the senses. If, then, the Word of God is in the world, which is a body, and has come upon the whole and every one of its parts, what is astonishing or absurd if we say that he has also come upon a human being?

For if it is altogether absurd that he should be in a body, it would also be absurd for him to come upon the universe and enlighten and move all things by his providence, since the whole universe too is a body.

But if it is fitting for him to come upon the world and be known in the whole, then it would also be fitting for him to appear in a human body and for that body to be enlightened and activated by him. For the human race is a part of the whole. And if the part is unfit to become his instrument for knowledge of the divinity, it would be still more absurd for him to be known through the whole world.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius turns from Jewish objections to a philosophical argument addressed to Greek critics.
His central analogy is that if the divine Word is present and active in the cosmos as a whole, presence in one human body is not intrinsically absurd.
